Issued at 151 AM EST Sat Nov 14 2026

Today-Sunday...The chilliest night and mornings for East Central 
Florida since March are expected this weekend. A series of cold 
fronts the last couple days associated with a substantial low 
pressure system lifting northeast from New England and the 
Canadian Maritimes have delivered progressively cooler and drier 
air. NBM statistics show a bimodal distribution of low 
temperatures across the members, with the lower cluster near the 
official forecast, and the other cluster 5-10 degrees warmer. The 
warmer temperatures are possible where overnight northerly winds 
hold closer to 10 mph and mixing counters radiational cooling and 
advection. MOS guidance continues signal low temperatures close to
the NBM 10th percentile (L-M40s) and would only be realized where
winds go light. The official forecast calls for temperatures to 
drop to the M40s-M50s for a couple hours prior to sunrise, coldest
inland and mildest along the Space and Treasure Coasts. Wind 
chills are forecast to sink to the L40-M40s for those couple 
couple hours before sunrise across all but the I-95 corridor of 
the Space and Treasure Coasts, and portions of the southernmost 
counties. Temperatures this afternoon only climb into the 60s, 
approaching 70 along the southern coast. Winds pick up to around 
10 mph with gusts to 20 mph.

High pressure at the surface behind the front builds towards the 
eastern seaboard Saturday night into Sunday, which starts to shift
winds onshore (NE). Temperatures at inland locations are again 
forecast to drop to the M-U40s for a couple hours before sunrise 
Sunday morning, but along the coast onshore flow will have already
started the warming trend, where lows are forecast in the 50s, 
approaching 60 on the southern coast. Wind chills again sink to 
the L-M40s across the interior. Afternoon temperatures Sunday are 
back in the 70s. Gentle winds may be gusty at times.

Dry through the period with low relative humidity and mostly 
clear skies. There is a Moderate Risk of dangerous rip currents at
the beaches. Always swim near the lifeguard, and never swim alone
if you enter the surf during this chilly weekend.

Monday-Tuesday...Aloft, deep troughing over the Atlantic seaboard
gradually shifts offshore and a broad ridge amplifies while 
moving over the eastern half of the CONUS. At the surface, high 
pressure will settle over the eastern US with the southern flank 
draped across the Florida peninsula, shifting onshore winds more 
easterly. A couple lobes of vorticity are expected to undercut the
ridge, sliding from the trough in the western US across the south
central US and toward the southeast while developing a weak 
surface disturbance. This disturbance is forecast to wash out as 
it moves into the Gulf, but will help to tighten the pressure 
gradient across the area between the high pressure to the north 
and the frontal boundaries stalled to the south, while also 
delivering some moisture into an otherwise dry airmass. Low 
chances (20% or less) for onshore moving shower return to the 
coast Monday, then increase to 20-50% and push farther inland 
Tuesday. Isolated lightning storms are not expected Monday, then 
low (20% or less) chances return Tuesday. Will need to monitor the
potential for heavy rainfall very closely due to how sensitive 
parts of ECFL are after previous extreme rainfall, but right now 
it's too far out to tell where if any threats may develop. Breezy 
and gusty conditions forecast as winds increase to 10-15 mph with 
gusts to 25 mph in the afternoons. Winds inland settle to around 
10 mph with less frequent gusts overnight, but along the coast 
will remain breezy and gusty. Gradual warming but temperatures 
stay near to below normal, with highs in the 70s and lows in the 
50s and 60s. Poor to hazardous beach and marine conditions will be
possible.

Wednesday-Friday...Decent model agreement in the overall upper
level pattern, driven by persistent troughing over the western US,
but there is some uncertainty where a low pressure system may 
develop in the adjacent Atlantic waters that could produce local 
coastal impacts. East of the Rockies, ridging aloft is shunted 
southeast by mid- upper level troughing sliding across the 
northern Plains towards the Great Lakes, causing the ridge to 
cutoff the trough over the Atlantic waters east of the ridge. The 
extent to which the ridge is suppressed, and where the cutoff low 
over the Atlantic develops remains uncertain. Surface high 
pressure should remain anchored to the eastern seaboard with 
Florida under the southern flank, but how tight the pressure 
gradient stays or becomes, depends on development and evolution of
the cut-off low. A tighter pressure gradient would result 
stronger onshore flow that could produce hazardous beach and 
marine conditions. At this juncture all models keep the highest 
moisture and heaviest rainfall over the Atlantic, but will need to
